source.title: Capability Salience Vector: Fine-grained Alignment of Loss and Capabilities for Downstream Task Scaling Law
source.authors: Qi-Ming Ge; Shu-Hao Xing; Song-Yang Gao; Yunhua Zhou; Yicheng Zou; Song-Yang Zhang; Zhi Chen; Hang Yan; Qi Zhang; Qi-Peng Guo; Kai Chen

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figure text and parts of the extracted layout are garbled, so figure-only numerical values were not inferred.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether loss-based measures predict downstream task performance, using a learned token-weighted loss and sigmoid fits rather than the original parameter/token/compute power-law measurement.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for learned Capability Salience Vector (CSV) loss and its comparisons with average-token and label-token loss, so these are recorded. It also explicitly reports that different data distributions yield different downstream scores at equal FLOPs and that models can have different task scores at the same average loss. Cited results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether downstream benchmark accuracy can be predicted from compute or from average token loss. Figures 1–2 and the all-token and label-token baselines in Table 1 say not reliably across data distributions and model families. It then proposes a learned token-weighted loss (CSV) that does predict scores for larger held-out models, which argues that V6 needs restating.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that compute and plain average validation loss cannot directly model downstream scaling across data distributions and model families. Weighting token losses with a learned Capability Salience Vector restores a predictable sigmoid loss-to-accuracy relation, with test MSE around 1e-3, and works for in-house checkpoints.
record.recipe_differences: The study learns token weights for capability-specific loss and fits sigmoid functions to downstream benchmark scores. It does not reproduce parameter/token/compute power-law fits or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction is reported to vary with validation-set data diversity; the authors recommend using more diverse validation text. The paper also reports task-dependent performance, including a task where all-token loss has lower test MSE than CSV.
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2025
record.problems: The study evaluates six benchmarks, and its authors note that benchmark coverage is limited. Exact values for several plotted comparisons are not available in the extracted text; reported MSEs have no uncertainty estimates. The text also notes that CSV effectiveness varies across optimization texts.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted. Per-model benchmark scores in Tables 3 and 4 are downstream evaluation results, not separate tests of loss-based prediction; the paper's prediction comparisons are reported as aggregate MSEs in Table 1 and plots.

untested.parts: Whether downstream accuracy is predictable from compute within a single fixed data distribution. Power-law form of the downstream relation. Tasks beyond the six objective benchmarks.
Whole version; no fitted exponents compared.

missing.what: In Figure 1 the text singles out only Hellaswag and BBH as differing at equal compute. Whether MMLU and GSM8K curves coincide across the data mixes is not stated and has no row.
Train and validation MSE per task for the CSV fits are shown in Figures 4–7 but garbled in the extracted text.

record.verdict_notes: The CSV rows are the study's own method, fitted on downstream scores of the smaller models. They support a restated V6 (downstream performance is predictable from appropriately weighted loss) rather than plain V6. The model families mix base and chat/SFT models. MSE values have no uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep tests held-out pretraining cross-entropy power laws in parameter count, tokens, or compute.
The paper predicts downstream benchmark scores, not the loss of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is measured.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling-law test.

Tests prediction of benchmark performance from loss-derived scores and across model sizes/families; does not establish a general power-law relation between downstream performance and scale or pretraining loss.
Does not compare power-law exponents or compute-optimal splits under alternative parameter-counting, schedules, or fitting methods.
